draft.title: Summary and indictable offences
card: a minor offence, such as offensive language or a minor traffic offence. It is heard by a magistrate in the Local Court, with no jury.
a serious offence, such as murder, armed robbery or large-scale drug supply. It can be tried by a judge and jury in a higher court.
Many indictable offences start in the Local Court, where a magistrate handles early steps. The most serious ones then go to a higher court for trial.
The type of offence depends on how serious the law treats it. It does not depend on how the accused pleads or how long the case takes.
draft.remember: Minor offences go to a magistrate. Serious offences can go to a judge and jury.

a.q: Which feature is usually true of a summary offence?
opts: It is heard by a magistrate without a jury
It is tried by a judge and jury
It is heard only in the Supreme Court
It is decided by the police, not a court
a.why: Summary offences are minor and are heard by a magistrate alone. A jury is linked to indictable offences, so the second option is the tempting mistake.
a.clue: Think about who hears minor matters and whether a jury is used.

b.q: Dev is charged with armed robbery, a serious offence. How is his offence best classed, and why?
opts: Indictable, because it is serious and can go before a jury
Summary, because it is first mentioned in the Local Court
Summary, because Dev may plead guilty to the charge
Indictable, because a magistrate must decide the outcome
b.why: Armed robbery is serious, so it is indictable and can be tried by a judge and jury. Appearing first in the Local Court does not make an offence summary, because many indictable offences begin there.
b.clue: Classing depends on how serious the offence is, not where it first appears.

a.best: It is heard by a magistrate without a jury

b.best: Indictable, because it is serious and can go before a jury

problems.detail: The stem already calls armed robbery 'a serious offence', and the clue says classing depends on seriousness. Together they hand students the answer without testing whether they know armed robbery is indictable. Drop 'a serious offence' from the stem, or soften the clue.
The distractor 'a magistrate must decide the outcome' uses 'must' where the card uses 'can'. Absolute words in distractors let test-wise students rule options out without knowing the idea.
